analysis.one_liner: Freezes all new endangered species listings and habitat protections until the law is reauthorized.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it died in the Environment and Public Works Committee after a single hearing, leaving existing endangered species protections in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Endangered Species Act to stop the Interior Department from adding any new species to the endangered or threatened lists, and from designating any critical habitat, until Congress reauthorized the law [S2][S3]. It also would have exempted federal agencies from their duty to protect listed species and to avoid actions that jeopardize them or destroy their habitat during that same period [S2][S3]. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and never received a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners, developers, and resource industries whose property or projects are restricted by endangered species listings and critical habitat designations would have gained, since new restrictions would be frozen and federal projects would no longer have to avoid harming species or habitat [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have barred the Interior Secretary from listing any new species as endangered or threatened, and from designating critical habitat, until the first reauthorization of the Endangered Species Act [S2][S3].

It would have exempted federal agencies from conservation programs and from the requirement that their actions not jeopardize listed species or destroy habitat, removing a layer of review from federally permitted or funded projects until reauthorization [S2][S3].

Sponsors framed the bill as protecting private property rights and shielding farmers, ranchers, and homeowners from economic losses caused by species listings and critical habitat designations [S1][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would have borne the cost: species identified as imperiled would go unprotected and their habitat unprotected during the freeze, and federal agencies would no longer be required to avoid actions that push species toward extinction [S2][S3]. Because the freeze ran until reauthorization rather than a fixed date, it had no guaranteed end point.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through lost species and habitat protections

drawbacks.text: An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill had no end date of its own: the freeze lasted until reauthorization, which Congress controlled, so protections could have been suspended indefinitely [S2][S3].

The freeze was total: it would have blocked listings for every species, including ones scientists had already determined were in danger, rather than targeting individual decisions landowners objected to [S2][S3].

The bill addressed a real grievance: species listings and habitat designations can restrict how landowners use their own property and reduce its value, with no compensation under existing law, and ranchers and farmers bore much of that burden [S1][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The property-rights concern behind the bill was genuine, but the remedy was a blunt, open-ended freeze on all new species protections and all federal conservation duties, with no timeline guaranteeing it would ever end. Weighing a temporary economic relief for landowners against an indefinite pause in protecting imperiled species, the costs to the public outweighed the benefits as drafted.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in March 1995, and was never reported out for a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, with original cosponsors including Sens. Lott, Gramm, Grassley, and Nickles, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S3][S5].
The subcommittee on Water, Fisheries, and Wildlife held hearings on March 7, 1995 — the only recorded action after referral [S5].
The full committee never reported the bill to the Senate, and it received no floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, existing Endangered Species Act protections — new listings, critical habitat designations, and federal agencies' duty to avoid harming species — stayed in place. The public and conservation interests kept those protections; the developers, ranchers, and resource industries the bill was written for did not get the freeze.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept endangered species protections

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill, held one subcommittee hearing, and never reported it to the full Senate for a vote.

against.name: Environmental and conservation organizations
against.role: National conservation groups active in the 1995 Endangered Species Act reauthorization fight
against.what_they_did: Opposed the wave of Endangered Species Act suspension and rollback bills in the 104th Congress, including listing moratoria.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored the bill; it died in a committee chaired by a moderate Republican without a floor vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: A freeze on new listings and critical habitat designations would have removed the main tool that restricts development on land where imperiled species live. The industry's gain came directly at the cost of the public's environmental protections.

Listings and habitat designations can restrict farming and grazing practices and land values; the bill was framed specifically around shielding farms and ranches from those costs. Sponsors argued existing law offered no compensation for those losses.

industries.industry: Timber, mining, and oil and gas on federal land
industries.note: Exempting federal agencies from the duty to avoid jeopardizing species or destroying habitat would have eased approval of federally permitted extraction and logging projects on public land.

The bill would have suspended the mechanisms that add species to the protected lists and shield their habitat, an outcome conservationists and the outdoor public would have lost under. It never passed, so the sector kept the status quo.
